transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Cora Vekulman.
Alaska's U.S. Senate race remains outstanding.
Democratic challenger Mary Peltola has increased her lead
over Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Alaska public media's Liz Ruskin reports Peltola
is nearly two percentage points ahead.
Peltola has 49% of the vote.
Her lead over Sullivan is now greater
than the vote total of the other candidate
named Dan Sullivan.
If that holds, it would undermine President Trump's claim
that the senator would be ahead,
if not for voter confusion over the two Sullivans.
Peltola's campaign manager said by email
her team is exceptionally confident Peltola
will be elected.
Sullivan's team did not issue an immediate statement
after the results update.
The Associated Press estimates more than 80%
of Alaska's vote is now counted.
More results are expected Friday.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
The U.S. Senate race in Mississippi
still hasn't been called either.
Democratic challenger Scott Cullum has increased his lead
to about 3,000 votes over Republican incumbent
Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The Ebola case count in Democratic Republic of the Congo
is now over 11,000 people.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports.
About half of those 11,000 people who got Ebola have died,
making this the deadliest outbreak in DRC's history.
Violence in parts of the country
has disrupted the outbreak response.
Just last week, militants affiliated with the Islamic State
burned down a treatment center near Breni,
killing nearly 50 people, according to health officials.
Given the rampant spread,
the humanitarian organization MSF
is urging the World Health Organization
to approve wider use of Ervibo.
It's a vaccine licensed for another species of Ebola,
but not the one behind this outbreak.
Clinical trials are ongoing,
but results are many weeks away.
There has been some good news.
The last of nine Ebola patients in Kenya
was discharged this week,
starting the 42-day countdown to certify
that the country is Ebola-free.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
The New York Federal Reserve finds credit card debt
increased across U.S. households over the summer,
and PR Stephen Bizaha reports they're better
keeping up with payments.
Households added another $52 billion in credit card debt
by September compared to a year earlier.
That brings the total debt to just under $1.3 trillion.
New York Fed researchers found a slight drop
in how much of that debt is considered seriously delinquent.
They also reported a sharp rise in consumers
borrowing against houses.
Home equity loan balances grew by about $23 billion
July through September, the largest increase since 2005.
Fed researchers say that's likely driven by home owners
having a lot of equity built up in their homes
and using that to borrow money at cheaper rates.
Stephen Bizaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
You're listening to NPR News.
Today is Veterans Day.
President Trump is scheduled to visit
Arlington National Cemetery to participate
in a wreath-laying ceremony.
President Trump will also deliver Veterans Day remarks.
Democrats in Congress say they plan to reverse
steep cuts to Medicaid when they retake control
of the House and Senate in January.
The changes take effect with the new year
and PR Selena Simmons-Duffin has more.
Medicaid provides health coverage
for about 70 million Americans with low incomes.
It's run by states, which have created new IT systems
at breakneck speed this past year.
That's because on January 1st, states will have to check
whether certain people are meeting new work requirements
or have a medical condition that exempts them.
Larry Levitt is with the nonprofit
health research organization KFF.
These work requirements start January 1st
and there's enormous uncertainty swirling around them,
not just the politics, but what's gonna happen
when states turn on the switch
and begin implementing this requirement.
Advocates in Nebraska, where the rules
have already taken effect, say the change there
has been chaotic and confusing.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
Ukrainian and Russian negotiators say they see some progress
in two days of talks in Abu Dhabi.
The discussions are mediated by the U.S.
President Trump's envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkov,
say they'll now travel to Moscow
to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Later, they'll meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
This is NPR News.
